claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Coulondre et al., 1978; Bird, 1980).

claims.claim: DNA methylation selectively reduces CpG dinucleotide frequencies in both plant and vertebrate genomes where DNA methylation is extensive.
claims.source: This selectively reduces CpG dinucleotide frequencies in both plant and vertebrate genomes where DNA methylation is extensive (Coulondre et al., 1978; Bird, 1980).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Most small DNA viruses and viruses with single stranded RNA genomes appear to mimic host-cell mRNA dinucleotide frequencies.
claims.source: Most small DNA viruses and viruses with single stranded RNA genomes appear to mimic host-cell mRNA dinucleotide frequencies, with a strong bias in both UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies in viruses of plants and vertebrates (Simmonds et al., 2013; Karlin et al., 1994; Rima and McFerran, 1997).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The genome of many invertebrates lack methylation and consequently show little if any suppression of CpG dinucleotide frequencies.
claims.source: In contrast, the genome of many invertebrates lack methylation and consequently show little if any suppression of CpG dinucleotide frequencies.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature (Lobo et al., 2009; Simmonds et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The genomes of viruses that infect invertebrates show little suppression of CpG.
claims.source: Consistent with the hypothesis for virus mimicry, the genomes of viruses that infect invertebrates show little suppression of CpG (Lobo et al., 2009; Simmonds et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: Increasing CpG or UpA dinucleotides in coding regions of echovirus7 while keeping protein coding identical strongly attenuated E7 independently of classical antiviral signalling pathways.
claims.source: For example, increasing CpG or UpA dinucleotides in coding regions of echovirus7 (E7, enterovirus, Picornaviridae) while keeping protein coding identical strongly attenuated E7 independently of classical antiviral signalling pathways, whereas removing CpG and UpA dinucleotides increased viral replication rates in vitro beyond those of WT virus (Atkinson et al., 2014; Witteveldt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: Removing CpG and UpA dinucleotides increased viral replication rates in vitro beyond those of WT virus.
claims.source: For example, increasing CpG or UpA dinucleotides in coding regions of echovirus7 (E7, enterovirus, Picornaviridae) while keeping protein coding identical strongly attenuated E7 independently of classical antiviral signalling pathways, whereas removing CpG and UpA dinucleotides increased viral replication rates in vitro beyond those of WT virus (Atkinson et al., 2014; Witteveldt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: Infections with influenza virus with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies were entirely non-pathogenic in mice and viral loads were markedly reduced.
claims.source: In mice, infections with influenza virus (Influenzavirus A, Orthomyxoviridae) with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies were entirely non-pathogenic and viral loads were markedly reduced.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Gaunt et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Infections with influenza virus with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies elicited inflammatory cytokine production and T-cell and antibody responses equal to or exceeding that of wild type virus.
claims.source: Such infections did however elicit inflammatory cytokine production and T-cell and antibody responses equal to or exceeding that of wild type virus and conferred complete protection from a lethal challenge dose of wild type influenza virus (Gaunt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Infections with influenza virus with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies conferred complete protection from a lethal challenge dose of wild type influenza virus.
claims.source: Such infections did however elicit inflammatory cytokine production and T-cell and antibody responses equal to or exceeding that of wild type virus and conferred complete protection from a lethal challenge dose of wild type influenza virus (Gaunt et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claims.claim: Alteration of CpG and UpA frequencies in viruses may introduce normally unfavoured codons or codon pairs that reduce translation rates.
claims.source: Such changes may have the secondary effect of introducing normally unfavoured codons or codon pairs in viral genomes, reducing translation rates that may cause further virus attenuation (Martínez et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents a hypothesis being tested in the current study.

claims.claim: In the E7 picornavirus model, dinucleotide frequency changes were the primary factor behind attenuation rather than codon pair bias.
claims.source: When done in the E7 picornavirus model, we found it was dinucleotide frequency changes that were the primary factor behind attenuation (Tulloch et al., 2014), although this conclusion has been disputed (Futcher et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors, though noted as disputed.

claims.claim: Upon entry into the host cell the viral genomic RNA of E7 is quickly released into the cytoplasm.
claims.source: Upon entry into the host cell the viral genomic RNA is quickly released into the cytoplasm.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about enterovirus replication.

claims.claim: E7 viral RNA is translated through a cap-independent mechanism into a single polyprotein that is further processed.
claims.source: Through a cap-independent mechanism viral RNA is translated into a single polyprotein that is further processed.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about enterovirus replication.

claims.claim: E7 RNA replication occurs in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) associated vesicles.
claims.source: RNA replication occurs in endoplasmic reticulum (ER) associated vesicles, where from a negative-sense RNA intermediate progeny positive-sense RNA genomes are transcribed.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about enterovirus replication.

claims.claim: The dsRNA replication intermediate is a known activator of cytosolic pattern recognition receptors, such as RIG-I and MDA5.
claims.source: The dsRNA replication intermediate is a known activator of cytosolic pattern recognition receptors, such as retinoic acid-inducible gene I (RIG-I) and melanoma differentiation-associated gene 5 (MDA5) (Baum et al., 2010; Peisley et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: The induction and secretion of interferon induces expression of a large number of cellular genes whose expression leads to the induction of an antiviral state within the cell.
claims.source: The consequent induction and secretion of interferon induces expression of a large number of cellular genes whose expression leads to the induction of an antiviral state within the cell (Randall and Goodbourn, 2008).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claims.claim: Viral titres of E7 with R2_U or R2_C were consistently lower compared to WT E7 across different cell types.
claims.source: Twenty-four hours post infection with the E7 R2 mutant viruses, infectious progeny virus was measured with an end point dilution assay (EPDA). Across the different cell types, the viral titres of E7 with R2_U or R2_C were consistently lower compared to WT E7 (Figure 1B, one-way ANOVA, p<0.01,).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The relative replication rates (RRRs) of E7 mutants differed between cell types.
claims.source: The relative replication rates (RRRs; ratio of TCID50s of mutant/WT virus) of E7 mutants differed between cell types.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B showing different RRR values across cell lines.

claims.claim: In RD cells R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.1.
claims.source: In RD cells (human muscle) and A549 cells (human lung epithelium) R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.1 and 0.4 respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: In A549 cells R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.4.
claims.source: In RD cells (human muscle) and A549 cells (human lung epithelium) R2_U E7 displayed an RRR of 0.1 and 0.4 respectively.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The RRR of R2_C was 0.01 in RD and A549 cells.
claims.source: The RRR of R2_C was further suppressed to 0.01 in these cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Cells that originated from the kidney displayed a more moderate E7 R2_C RRR of approximately 0.09.
claims.source: Cells that originated from the kidney displayed a more moderate E7 R2_C RRR of approximately 0.09 (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: There was no relationship between RRR and virus titre of WT virus at 24 hr.
claims.source: However, there was no relationship between RRR (Figure 1C, x-axis) and virus titre of WT virus at 24 hr (Figure 1C, y-axis, representing cell susceptibility; Pearson correlation coefficient CpG −0.57 and UpA −0.63).
claims.evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis of data shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: A549 cells expressing BVDV NPro showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
claims.source: These included A549 cells expressing the bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV, genus Pestivirus) N-terminal protease fragment (NPro), which blocks the activity of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF-3)(Hilton et al., 2006) and IRF7 (Fiebach et al., 2011) or the hepatitis C virus (HCV, genus Hepacivirus) protein NS3/4A that inhibits cytokine gene expression by cleavage of IPS-1/MAVS/VISA/Cardif (Kaukinen et al., 2006). Both cell lines showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B showing RRR values for A549-Npro cells.

claims.claim: A549 cells expressing HCV NS3/4A showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
claims.source: These included A549 cells expressing the bovine viral diarrhoea virus (BVDV, genus Pestivirus) N-terminal protease fragment (NPro), which blocks the activity of interferon regulatory factor 3 (IRF-3)(Hilton et al., 2006) and IRF7 (Fiebach et al., 2011) or the hepatitis C virus (HCV, genus Hepacivirus) protein NS3/4A that inhibits cytokine gene expression by cleavage of IPS-1/MAVS/VISA/Cardif (Kaukinen et al., 2006). Both cell lines showed similar or greater restriction in replication for both CpG- and UpA-high mutants compared to the parental cell line.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B showing RRR values for A549 NS3/4A cells.

claims.claim: Vero cells restricted mutated E7 viruses comparable to that of other cultured kidney cells tested with a more moderate attenuation of the CpG high virus.
claims.source: The monkey kidney fibroblast cell line, Vero, which has intact IFN signalling pathways but cannot produce type 1 IFNs (Desmyter et al., 1968), restricted mutated E7 viruses comparable to that of other cultured kidney cells tested in this study with a more moderate attenuation between of the CpG high virus (Figure 1BC).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 1B and 1C.

claims.claim: Reduced replication of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies occurs in all the tested cell types.
claims.source: Together this indicates that reduced replication of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies occurs in all the tested cell types and restriction cannot be lifted by inhibiting some of the most potent antiviral signalling cascades.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 1 showing consistent attenuation across cell types.

claims.claim: Restriction of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies cannot be lifted by inhibiting some of the most potent antiviral signalling cascades.
claims.source: Together this indicates that reduced replication of E7 with increased UpA and CpG dinucleotide frequencies occurs in all the tested cell types and restriction cannot be lifted by inhibiting some of the most potent antiviral signalling cascades.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data showing attenuation persists in cells with inhibited IRF3 and MAVS pathways (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: A permutated mutant of E7, with the native sequences of R1 or R2 scrambled but retaining coding and native dinucleotide frequencies, showed WT levels of replication.
claims.source: This was supported by a high synonymous site variability and low mean folding energies (Atkinson et al., 2014). In these experiments a permutated mutant of E7, with the native sequences of R1 or R2 scrambled but retaining coding and native dinucleotide frequencies, showed WT levels of replication, indicative that these genome region can be safely modified without consequences for viral replication (Atkinson et al., 2014; Tulloch et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: Synonymous removal of all possible CpG and UpA dinucleotides from firefly luciferase strongly increased the replication rate of the E7luc replicon.
claims.source: Being of insect origin, the wild type firefly luciferase gene (luc_WT) contains a relatively high ratio of CpG dinucleotides (CpG 1.210 and UpA 0.695 observed/expected). Synonymous removal of all possible CpG and UpA dinucleotides from firefly luciferase (luc_cu, ratio CpG 0.013 and UpA 0.154 O/E) strongly increased the replication rate of the E7luc replicon (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Addition of the 1242 nucleotide long ncR1 of WT composition to the E7 replicon RNA had no effect on replication compared to that of the E7 replicon without ncR1.
claims.source: Addition of the 1242 nucleotide long ncR1 of WT composition to the E7 replicon RNA had no effect on replication compared to that of the E7 replicon without ncR1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The replication structures in the 3'-UTR are not affected by the addition of 1242 nucleotides to the 5'-end of the 3'-UTR.
claims.source: This indicates that the replication structures in the 3'-UTR are not affected by the addition of 1242 nucleotides to the 5'-end of the 3'-UTR.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the observation that adding ncR1 does not affect replication.

claims.claim: RNA replication rates of E7 replicons with a high UpA ncR1 tail in RD and A549 cells showed mildly reduced relative replication rates (to 0.5).
claims.source: However, RNA replication rates of E7 replicons with a high UpA ncR1 tail (ncR1_U) in RD and A549 cells showed mildly reduced relative replication rates (to 0.5), whereas the high CpG sequence, ncR1_C, reduced replication rates by approximately 10-fold at 6 and 9 hr post RNA transfection (hpt) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The high CpG sequence ncR1_C reduced replication rates by approximately 10-fold at 6 and 9 hr post RNA transfection.
claims.source: However, RNA replication rates of E7 replicons with a high UpA ncR1 tail (ncR1_U) in RD and A549 cells showed mildly reduced relative replication rates (to 0.5), whereas the high CpG sequence, ncR1_C, reduced replication rates by approximately 10-fold at 6 and 9 hr post RNA transfection (hpt) (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Similar degrees of attenuation were observed in replicons where CpG and UpA frequencies were increased through mutation of the coding region in R2.
claims.source: Similar degrees of attenuation were observed in replicons where CpG and UpA frequencies were increased through mutation of the coding region in R2 (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B comparing coding and non-coding region mutants.

claims.claim: The RRRs of both coding and non-coding CpG- and UpA-mutants approached that of WT in kidney-derived BHK cells.
claims.source: In contrast, the RRRs of both coding and non-coding CpG- and UpA-mutants approached that of WT in kidney-derived BHK cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: No effects on replication were observed in replicons with ncR1 (non-coding) or R2 (coding) sequences possessing lower (cu) CpG/UpA frequencies than WT.
claims.source: No effects on replication were observed in replicons with ncR1 (non-coding) or R2 (coding) sequences possessing lower (cu) CpG/UpA frequencies than WT (Figure 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: Kinase inhibitor C16 was able to largely reverse the attenuation of CpG- and UpA-high mutants of E7 virus, independently of PKR.
claims.source: We previously reported that kinase inhibitor C16 was able to largely reverse the attenuation of CpG- and UpA-high mutants of E7 virus, independently of PKR (Atkinson et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claims.claim: The relative luciferase expression of E7 replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotides in their ncR1 were increased by 1.8 and 6 fold respectively in the presence of C16.
claims.source: The relative luciferase expression of E7 replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotides in their ncR1 were increased by 1.8 and 6 fold respectively in the presence of C16 while the replication of WT and CDLR was unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, p-values 0.069 and 0.01, T-test).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: The observed reversal of attenuation of the E7 ncR1 variants by C16 closely resembled that of viruses with modifications in the coding region.
claims.source: The observed reversal of attenuation of the E7 ncR1 variants closely resembled that of viruses with modifications in the coding region (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and provides evidence that the mechanisms of attenuation in the two systems were similar.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 comparing replicons and viruses.

claims.claim: The replicon with ncR1_C showed an RRR of approximately 0.1 in A549 and RD cells.
claims.source: The replicon with ncR1_C showed an RRR of approximately 0.1 in A549 and RD cells, a greater degree of attenuation than observed in the kidney-derived 293, 293T and Vero cells, while attenuation in the pathway knockout cells, A549-V and A549 NS3/4A was greater (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: The ranking of cell lines for attenuation of both CpG and UpA-elevated mutants was similar between the virus and replicon challenge systems.
claims.source: Although the overall degree of attenuation in the replicon format was lower than in the low MOI infection experiments performed for infectious virus (Figure 1B), the ranking of cell lines for attenuation of both CpG and UpA-elevated mutants was similar between the two challenge systems (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by comparison of data in Figures 1B and 3B.

claims.claim: In all murine cell types, replication rates of replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies in the non-coding region were consistently lower than WT.
claims.source: At six hpt, samples were lysed and assayed for luciferase expression. In all cell types replication rates of replicons with increased UpA or CpG dinucleotide frequencies in the non-coding region were consistently lower than WT (RRRs ranging from 0.01 to 0.3 for ncR1_C and 0.2–0.7 for ncR1_U).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Replicon mutants with an ncR1 of P or cu composition invariably showed equivalent replication to WT in murine cells.
claims.source: In contrast, replicon mutants with an ncR1 of P or cu composition invariably showed equivalent replication to WT (Figure 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: GuHCl effectively inhibits picornavirus RNA replication through inhibiting initiation of negative strand RNA synthesis and RNA strand elongation.
claims.source: It is well established that GuHCl effectively inhibits picornavirus RNA replication through inhibiting initiation of negative strand RNA synthesis and RNA strand elongation (Barton and Flanegan, 1997; Pfister and Wimmer, 1999).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claims.claim: GuHCl treatment or mutation of the viral polymerase similarly reduced luciferase readings throughout the time-course experiment, with no sign of replicon RNA replication.
claims.source: GuHCl treatment or mutation of the viral polymerase similarly reduced luciferase readings throughout the time-course experiment, with no sign of replicon RNA replication.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C.

claims.claim: E7 replicons with CpG or UpA high ncR1 showed comparable luciferase expression as replicons with WT ncR1 sequences when replication was inhibited by either GuHCl or mutation of the viral polymerase.
claims.source: Importantly, E7 replicons with CpG or UpA high ncR1 showed comparable luciferase expression as replicons with WT ncR1 sequences when replication was inhibited by either GuHCl or mutation of the viral polymerase (Figure 4B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C showing no difference in translation between WT and mutant replicons when replication is blocked.

claims.claim: Untreated, replication competent replicons displayed the typical attenuation of luciferase expression in CpG and UpA mutants.
claims.source: Untreated, replication competent replicons displayed the typical attenuation of luciferase expression in CpG and UpA mutants (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: There was a modest, approximate 5-fold reduction in luciferase expression over the 24 hr course of the experiment observed in non-replicating replicons that may reflect partial degradation of the transfected RNA.
claims.source: There was a modest, approximate 5-fold reduction in luciferase expression over the 24 hr course of the experiment observed in non-replicating replicons that may reflect partial degradation of the transfected RNA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the data in Figure 4B and 4C showing declining luciferase over time in non-replicating conditions.

claims.claim: Reductions in luciferase expression were comparable between WT and CpG/UpA modified replicons in non-replicating conditions.
claims.source: Reductions in luciferase expression were comparable between WT and CpG/UpA modified replicons (Figure 4A–C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4B and 4C showing similar decay rates.

claims.claim: At six hours post transfection, replicating E7 replicon RNA with a CpG-high ncR1 displayed an approximate 10-fold reduction in luciferase expression when compared to WT.
claims.source: At six hours post transfection, replicating E7 replicon RNA with a CpG-high ncR1 displayed an approximate 10-fold reduction in luciferase expression when compared to WT (Figure 4D, gray bars).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: When replication was inhibited by GuHCl, translation from the CpG-high replicon RNA was comparable to that of the WT in all tested cell types.
claims.source: In contrast, when replication was inhibited by GuHCl, translation from the CpG-high replicon RNA was comparable to that of the WT in all tested cell types (Figure 4D, black bars).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4D showing similar translation efficiency when replication is blocked.

claims.claim: Replicons with UpA-modified ncR1 also expressed similar levels of luciferase compared to WT in a non-replicating context with ratios ranging from 0.5 to 2.9.
claims.source: Replicons with UpA-modified ncR1 also expressed similar levels of luciferase compared to WT in a non-replicating context with ratios ranging from 0.5 to 2.9 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The observed attenuation of UpA or CpG high replicon mutants is not dependent on differences in translation rates or instability of the coding region RNA sequences in the cell.
claims.source: Combined, these results demonstrate that the observed attenuation of UpA or CpG high replicon mutants is not dependent on differences in translation rates or instability of the coding region RNA sequences in the cell.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 4 showing no difference in translation efficiency between WT and mutant replicons when replication is blocked.

claims.claim: Replicons with the single CpG-high ncS showed significantly reduced E7 RNA replication.
claims.source: Transfection of these replicon RNAs with various compositions in their ncS regions into RD cells resulted in significantly reduced E7 RNA replication for the single CpG-high ncS (ncS_C) but not the single UpA-high ncS_U (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Replicons with the single UpA-high ncS did not show significantly reduced E7 RNA replication.
claims.source: Transfection of these replicon RNAs with various compositions in their ncS regions into RD cells resulted in significantly reduced E7 RNA replication for the single CpG-high ncS (ncS_C) but not the single UpA-high ncS_U (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: Replicons with the double ncS of both U and C composition showed significantly reduced replication compared to their respective single ncS replicons.
claims.source: However replicons with the double ncS of both U and C composition showed significantly reduced replication compared to their respective single ncS replicons (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B with statistical analysis.

claims.claim: Luciferase expression of the CpG-high double region mutant was little different from that of the non-replicative guanidine treated control, indicating that this longer insertion almost entirely abrogated replication of this construct.
claims.source: Indeed, luciferase expression of the CpG-high double region mutant was little different from that of the non-replicative guanidine treated control (Figure 5B; dotted red line), indicating that this longer insertion almost entirely abrogated replication of this construct.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5B comparing double CpG mutant to GuHCl control.

claims.claim: Cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs.
claims.source: Together the observations that cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs, but translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting indicates that codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined data in Figures 4 and 5.

claims.claim: CpG/UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting.
claims.source: Together the observations that cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs, but translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting indicates that codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 4 showing no difference in translation efficiency.

claims.claim: Codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
claims.source: Together the observations that cumulative CpG, and to a lesser extent UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions of E7 replicons have restricted RRRs, but translate equally efficiently in a non-replicating setting indicates that codon bias, codon pair bias or other direct effects on translational efficiency are not at the heart of the observed restriction.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined experimental results.

claims.claim: The restriction mechanism implies a cell-mediated restriction of viral RNA replication and/or an alternative fate of the compositionally altered (viral) RNA.
claims.source: Rather it implies a cell-mediated restriction of viral RNA replication and/or an alternative fate of the compositionally altered (viral) RNA.
claims.evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing restriction independent of translation effects.

claims.claim: Infection with equal RNA resulted in reduced infectivity of E7 R2_C virus as early as two hours post infection.
claims.source: Infection with equal RNA resulted in reduced infectivity of E7 R2_C virus as early as two hours post infection and a prolonged delay in the production of progeny virus and RNA levels (Figure 6).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6A showing reduced viral titers at early time points.

claims.claim: There was no difference in initial receptor binding/viral entry between the E7 variant R2_C and other mutants as the genomic RNA copies detected after washing off the inoculum were identical to the mean of all samples at 1 hr post infection.
claims.source: In this experiment there was no difference in initial receptor binding/viral entry between the E7 variant R2_C and other mutants as the genomic RNA copies detected after washing off the inoculum were identical to the mean of all samples at 1 hr post infection (mean 1.00, R2_C 1.00, R2_U 1.03 SD 0.04).
claims.evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing equal RNA levels at 1 hpi.

claims.claim: After the initial delay in RNA replication, E7 with increased CpG dinucleotide frequencies replicated at a rate similar to that of other E7 variants.
claims.source: Interestingly, after the initial delay in RNA replication, E7 with increased CpG dinucleotide frequencies replicated at a rate similar to that of other E7 variants (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 6B showing similar slopes after the initial delay.

claims.claim: Small localized foci with intracellular genomic E7 RNA were observed at two hpi in all infected cells at frequencies that were comparable between WT and mutant viruses.
claims.source: Small localized foci with intracellular genomic E7 RNA were observed at two hpi (Figure 7A, white arrowheads) in all infected cells at frequencies that were comparable between WT and mutant viruses.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: At four hours post infection, WT and R2_U mutants developed clear pockets of replication in a large percentage of cells, whereas detection of E7 RNA with increased CpG dinucleotides became less frequent.
claims.source: At four hours post infection, WT and R2_U mutants developed clear pockets of replication in a large percentage of cells, whereas detection of E7 RNA with increased CpG dinucleotides became less frequent.
claims.evidence: This is supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 7A.

claims.claim: At six hours, RNA replication of E7 R2_C had progressed to display similar fluorescent intensities compared to the other E7 variants, but only in 3.5% of cells, compared to 49% and 36% of cells infected with R2_WT or R2_U viruses, respectively.
claims.source: At six hours, RNA replication of E7 R2_C had progressed to display similar fluorescent intensities compared to the other E7 variants, but only in 3.5% of cells, compared to 49% and 36% of cells infected with R2_WT or R2_U viruses, respectively (Figure 7BC).
claims.evidence: This is supported by quantitative RNA FISH data in Figure 7C.

claims.claim: Dinucleotide frequency changes influenced the frequency of infected cells, but not necessarily their subsequent replication ability.
claims.source: The striking observation that dinucleotide frequency changes influenced the frequency of infected cells, but not necessarily their subsequent replication ability was verified by flow cytometry of a further set of E7 replicon constructs in which the luciferase gene was replaced by enhanced green fluorescent protein (EGFP).
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the RNA FISH data in Figure 7 and verified by FACS data in Figure 8.

claims.claim: FACS analysis showed that the percentage of EGFP expressing cells at 6 hpt differed dramatically between WT and CpG-high mutant replicons while the mean fluorescent intensities of the cells that were fluorescent was comparable.
claims.source: Similar to the above RNA FISH experiments, FACS analysis showed that the percentage of EGFP expressing cells at 6 hpt differed dramatically between WT and CpG-high mutant replicons while the mean fluorescent intensities of the cells that were fluorescent was comparable (Figure 8AB, Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and Table 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by FACS data in Figure 8A and 8B and Table 2.

claims.claim: Attenuation was enhanced for CpG- and UpA-high mutants when both coding R2 and ncR1 were modified.
claims.source: Attenuation was enhanced for CpG- and UpA-high mutants when both coding R2 and ncR1 were modified (Figure 8 and Table 2).

results.result: CpG and UpA dinucleotides are under-represented in the genomes of most RNA viruses infecting vertebrates and plants, mimicking host mRNA composition, while viruses infecting invertebrates show little CpG suppression consistent with the lack of methylation in invertebrate genomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C11-C13, C18-C20, and C114 collectively establish well-documented patterns of dinucleotide suppression in viral genomes. These claims are supported by multiple citations to prior literature (Simmonds et al., 2013; Karlin et al., 1994; Rima and McFerran, 1997) and represent established knowledge in the field. The correlation between host genome methylation patterns and viral CpG suppression is well-supported.

results.result: Artificially increasing CpG/UpA dinucleotides attenuates viruses through an unknown mechanism, while removing these dinucleotides increases viral replication rates. In mice, influenza virus with increased CpG/UpA was non-pathogenic but elicited protective immune responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C21-C25, and C115 establish prior work demonstrating viral attenuation by CpG/UpA modification. These are supported by citations to prior work (Atkinson et al., 2014; Witteveldt et al., 2016; Gaunt et al., 2016) and establish the knowledge gap that motivates the current study. The claims accurately represent findings from cited literature.

results.result: E7 viruses with increased CpG or UpA dinucleotides in R2 showed consistently lower viral titers across different cell types at 24 hours post-infection, with relative replication rates (RRRs) varying between cell types but showing no correlation with WT virus susceptibility.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C39 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 1B with appropriate statistical analysis (one-way ANOVA, p<0.01). The RRR values are quantified for multiple cell lines, and the lack of correlation between RRR and WT virus titer is demonstrated with Pearson correlation coefficients. The data are internally consistent and appropriately analyzed.

results.result: Restriction of E7 replication by increased CpG/UpA dinucleotides occurs in all tested cell types and cannot be lifted by inhibiting IRF3 or MAVS antiviral signaling pathways, including in cells expressing BVDV NPro or HCV NS3/4A.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 are supported by data in Figure 1B showing that attenuation persists in cells with inhibited antiviral pathways (A549-Npro, A549 NS3/4A, Vero). The observation that restriction occurs across all cell types despite pathway inhibition is well-documented. This is a key finding ruling out conventional interferon-mediated antiviral responses.

results.result: E7 replicons with CpG/UpA modifications in non-coding regions (ncR1) showed similar attenuation to coding region (R2) mutants in RD and A549 cells, with approximately 10-fold reduction for CpG-high and 2-fold for UpA-high sequences, while attenuation was reduced in BHK kidney cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C53 are supported by data in Figures 2 and 2-figure supplements showing comparable attenuation between coding and non-coding region mutants. The quantitative RRR values are provided, and the cell-type specific differences (particularly in BHK cells) are documented. This is a critical finding demonstrating that attenuation is independent of codon usage effects.

results.result: Kinase inhibitor C16 reversed the attenuation of CpG- and UpA-high mutants in both viruses and replicons, increasing luciferase expression by 1.8-fold for UpA-high and 6-fold for CpG-high replicons, independently of PKR.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C56 are supported by data in Figure 2-figure supplement 3 with statistical analysis (p-values 0.069 and 0.01). The reversal by C16 is demonstrated for both replicons and viruses, providing evidence that the restriction is not due to intrinsic defects in the mutant sequences. The similarity between replicon and virus responses validates the replicon system.

results.result: The ranking of cell lines for attenuation of CpG and UpA-elevated mutants was similar between virus and replicon systems across multiple human and murine cell types, with RRRs ranging from 0.01 to 0.3 for CpG-high and 0.2-0.7 for UpA-high in murine cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C60 are supported by data in Figures 3A-C showing consistent patterns across cell types and experimental systems. The comparison between virus and replicon systems (Figure 3B) validates the replicon approach. The extension to murine cells demonstrates the breadth of the restriction phenomenon. The quantitative RRR values are provided for multiple cell lines.

results.result: When replication was inhibited by GuHCl or polymerase mutation, E7 replicons with CpG or UpA high ncR1 showed comparable luciferase expression to WT, demonstrating that attenuation is not dependent on differences in translation rates or RNA stability.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C70, C76-C77 are strongly supported by data in Figure 4 showing no difference in translation efficiency between WT and mutant replicons when replication is blocked. This is a critical control experiment that definitively rules out translation efficiency as the mechanism of attenuation. The experiment is well-designed with appropriate controls (GuHCl treatment and polymerase mutants) and tested across multiple cell types (Figure 4D).

results.result: Cumulative CpG and UpA dinucleotides in non-coding regions have additive effects on E7 replication restriction, with double ncS insertions showing significantly greater attenuation than single insertions, and the CpG-high double mutant almost entirely abrogating replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C75 are supported by data in Figure 5B with statistical analysis showing significant differences. The dose-dependent effect of increasing CpG/UpA content provides strong evidence for a cumulative recognition mechanism. The comparison to GuHCl-treated controls (Figure 5B, dotted red line) provides appropriate context for the magnitude of attenuation.

results.result: Infection with equal RNA copies showed reduced infectivity of E7 R2_C virus as early as 2 hours post-infection with no difference in initial entry, but after the initial delay, CpG-high virus replicated at rates similar to other variants.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 are supported by data in Figure 6 showing early time-point analysis. The qRT-PCR data (C80) demonstrates equal RNA levels at 1 hpi, ruling out entry defects. The observation that replication rates normalize after initial delay (C81, Figure 6B) is an important finding suggesting the restriction acts at replication initiation rather than elongation.

results.result: RNA FISH analysis showed that while initial RNA foci were comparable between WT and mutant viruses at 2 hpi, CpG-high mutants failed to develop replication complexes in most cells, with only 3.5% of cells showing productive replication at 6 hpi compared to 49% for WT.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by RNA FISH data in Figure 7 with quantitative analysis (Figure 7C). The observation that dinucleotide frequency affects the frequency of productively infected cells but not the intensity of replication in positive cells is a key mechanistic finding. The imaging data are appropriately quantified and statistically analyzed.

results.result: FACS analysis of EGFP-expressing replicons confirmed that CpG-high mutants showed dramatically reduced percentages of positive cells while mean fluorescent intensities were comparable, with enhanced attenuation when both coding R2 and ncR1 were modified, and reduced attenuation in BHK cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 are supported by FACS data in Figure 8 and Table 2. This independent experimental approach confirms the RNA FISH findings (C85) and extends them to show additive effects of multiple modified regions. The data are quantified and statistically analyzed (Figure 8, asterisks indicate p<0.05). The BHK cell data are consistent with earlier findings.

results.result: The restriction in E7 replication occurs immediately after viral entry with incoming virions failing to form replication complexes, though a small number of cells can overcome restriction, suggesting either RNA defects or saturable restriction factors.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C89-C91 synthesize findings from Figures 6-8. The conclusion that restriction occurs post-entry but pre-replication complex formation is well-supported by the combined data. However, C91 includes speculation about mechanisms (RNA defects vs. saturable factors) that is not definitively tested. The core observation of early restriction is solid, but the mechanistic interpretation remains uncertain.

results.result: Sequencing of CpG/UpA-high virus stocks showed comparable mutation frequencies to WT (approximately 10^-4 mutations/nucleotide) with no evidence of RNA editing signatures, indicating these viral RNAs are not intrinsically replication defective.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C92-C95, C129-C130 are supported by sequencing data in Table 3. The mutation frequencies are comparable across all variants and consistent with published poliovirus rates. The absence of RNA editing signatures (no enrichment for A-G or C-U transitions) rules out ADAR/APOBEC-mediated defects. Combined with C16 reversal data, this strongly argues against intrinsic defects.

results.result: CpG/UpA-high viral RNAs were not differentially sequestered in cytoplasmic stress granules, with no G3BP-positive granules observed during E7 infection and no increased eIF2α phosphorylation compared to WT virus.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C97-C99 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 9 and Western blot data in Figure 9-figure supplement 1A. The absence of stress granule formation and eIF2α phosphorylation rules out stress response pathways as mediators of restriction. The controls (arsenite treatment) are appropriate.

results.result: Treatment with acriflavine (RNA interference inhibitor) did not affect RRR of mutants, and caspase 3/7 activity correlated with viral replication rates rather than CpG/UpA content, ruling out RNA interference and apoptosis as restriction mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C102 are supported by data in Figure 9-figure supplement 1B-C. The ACF experiment rules out RNA interference pathways, and the caspase assay demonstrates that apoptosis is a consequence of replication rather than a cause of restriction. These are appropriate negative controls that narrow down possible mechanisms.

results.result: CpG/UpA-high RNAs did not induce a systemic antiviral state, as demonstrated by trans-infection experiments showing no effect on WT virus replication, indicating restriction acts strictly in cis and differs from conventional interferon-mediated responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C105-C109, C118 are supported by data in Figure 10 showing no trans effects in three different experimental formats (plasmid expression, co-transfection of non-replicating RNA, co-transfection of replicons). This is a critical finding that distinguishes the restriction mechanism from conventional antiviral responses. The experimental design is rigorous with appropriate controls.

results.result: Viruses with increased CpG/UpA frequencies do not differentially induce stress, interferon-coupled, or apoptosis-associated antiviral pathways, and the restriction mechanism appears to lie outside the conventional paradigm of innate cellular immune pathways.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C104, C140-C141, C149-C152, C156-C157, C167 synthesize negative results from multiple experiments (Figures 1, 9, 10, and cited prior work). The systematic ruling out of conventional antiviral pathways (IRF3, MAVS, TLR7/8, interferon response, stress granules, apoptosis) is well-documented. The conclusion that restriction lies outside conventional paradigms is justified by the comprehensive negative results.

results.result: The context of bases surrounding CpG dinucleotides has a potent effect on replication attenuation, with ncR1_UUCGUU showing 30-fold lower RRR than WT despite having identical CpG content, and ncR1_AACGAA showing RRR comparable to CpG-high sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C110-C113 are supported by data in Figure 11B showing dramatic context-dependent effects. This is an important finding demonstrating that CpG alone is not sufficient for recognition and that flanking sequences matter. However, only two contexts were tested (AACGAA and UUCGUU), limiting the ability to define minimal recognition motifs. Further work is needed to characterize the recognition sequence.

results.result: The functional constraints act directly on RNA with increased CpG and UpA dinucleotides to inhibit viral RNA replication, independent of whether these nucleotides are in coding or non-coding regions, demonstrating that attenuation is independent of codon usage or codon pair bias.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C116-C117, C120-C121, C124 represent the central conclusion of the study. This is well-supported by the combined data from Figures 2-5 showing comparable attenuation in coding and non-coding regions, and Figure 4 showing no translation defects. The conclusion that dinucleotide composition rather than codon usage drives attenuation is strongly supported for the E7 model.

results.result: Host cells possess intrinsic defense pathways that prevent replication of viruses with increased CpG/UpA frequencies independently of codon usage, mediated through cell-mediated restriction of viral RNA replication and/or alternative fate of compositionally altered RNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C9, C78, C96 represent the overarching conclusion of the study. This is supported by the combined evidence ruling out translation effects, intrinsic RNA defects, and conventional antiviral pathways, while demonstrating cis-acting restriction that occurs at replication initiation. The conclusion of host-cell restriction factors is well-justified, though the specific factors remain unidentified.

results.result: The findings suggest that under-representation of UpA and CpG dinucleotides in viral RNA has contributed to biases in nucleotide composition and codon choice in native viral sequences, potentially representing an evolutionarily conserved eukaryotic virus defense mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C123, C161, C168 represent speculation about evolutionary implications and generalizability beyond the E7 model. While the widespread CpG/UpA suppression in viral genomes (C1, C114, C160) supports evolutionary constraint, the specific mechanism identified in E7 has not been demonstrated in other viruses or organisms. The speculation about plant viruses (C161) is particularly uncertain given differences in antiviral mechanisms (C162-C163).

results.result: Prior work suggested that alteration of CpG/UpA frequencies may introduce unfavored codons reducing translation rates, but in the E7 model, dinucleotide frequency changes were the primary factor behind attenuation rather than codon pair bias, as demonstrated by permutated controls showing WT replication.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C45, C119 establish the context and rationale for the current study. The prior work by the authors (Tulloch et al., 2014) is cited, though noted as disputed (Futcher et al., 2015). The permutated control data showing WT replication validates that the R1/R2 regions can be modified without affecting replication, supporting the experimental design.

results.result: RNA virus genomes possess RNA secondary and tertiary structures that interact with host cell elements, and the E7 replication cycle involves cap-independent translation, ER-associated RNA replication, and dsRNA intermediates that activate cytosolic pattern recognition receptors.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C28-C32 provide established background knowledge about RNA virus biology and the E7 replication cycle. These are well-supported by citations to prior literature and represent standard knowledge in the field. This background is necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings.

results.result: UpA dinucleotides are recognized by RNA-degrading enzymes and may control RNA turnover, while CpG suppression results from methylation-induced deamination. RNase L can cleave UpA/UpU dinucleotides, potentially accounting for UpA suppression, though this doesn't explain why UpU is not similarly suppressed.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17, C136-C139 provide mechanistic background for dinucleotide suppression in host genomes. These are supported by citations to prior literature. The speculation about RNase L (C138) is reasonable but the observation about UpU (C139) highlights an inconsistency in this hypothesis. This background is relevant but the specific mechanisms may not apply to the E7 restriction.

results.result: While no currently described PRRs recognize CpGs in RNA, CpG dinucleotides in DNA activate TLR9, and removing CpGs from transgenes improves expression in vivo. TLR9-independent mechanisms exist for detecting CpG dinucleotides, and GU/AU-rich sequences activate TLR7/8.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C148 provide background on potential recognition mechanisms. These are supported by citations to prior literature. The observation of TLR9-independent CpG recognition (C146) is particularly relevant to the current findings. However, the relevance to the E7 system is limited as discussed in C149-C151.

results.result: Picornaviruses are well-armored against IFN-mediated responses through the 2C protease that cleaves MAVS, MDA5, and RIG-I. Inhibition of replication was observed immediately after infection before ISG induction, preventing establishment of replication complexes rather than inhibiting expression once formed.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C155, C158-C159 combine established knowledge about picornavirus immune evasion with experimental findings from Figures 6-8. The timing of restriction (before ISG induction) is well-documented and argues against interferon-mediated mechanisms. The distinction between preventing establishment vs. inhibiting ongoing replication is an important mechanistic insight.

results.result: While post-transcriptional RNA editing or increased intramolecular base pairing could theoretically cause replication defects, the reversal by C16 and reduced attenuation in BHK cells argues strongly against intrinsic replication defects in the mutant viruses.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C134 present and test alternative hypotheses for the restriction mechanism. The RNA editing hypothesis (C127-C128) is ruled out by sequencing data (Table 3, C129). The base-pairing hypothesis (C131) is ruled out by C16 reversal and cell-type differences (C132-C133). The logic is sound and the experimental evidence is compelling.

results.result: While viral RNA structure may serve as PAMPs for PRRs, and enterovirus 71 protein 3A suppresses RNA interference, there is nothing in siRNA mechanisms that would cause dinucleotide composition-related differences in replication efficacy, and animal and plant cells differ in their antiviral mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C135, C162-C166 discuss potential mechanisms and their limitations. The RNA interference pathway is considered (C164-C165) but reasonably dismissed (C166) based on mechanistic incompatibility. The discussion of differences between animal and plant antiviral responses (C162-C163) is relevant to the speculation about evolutionary conservation but highlights uncertainties in generalization.

results.result: Plant viruses suppress CpG and UpA dinucleotide frequencies as much or more intensively than vertebrate viruses.
results.evaluation: Claim C160 is supported by prior literature on viral genome composition (implied by citations in C1, C11, C114). This observation is important for the speculation about evolutionary conservation (C161) but is presented as established knowledge rather than a finding of the current study.
